edges.description: Without NIT1, dGSH formed by transaminase side reactions is not repaired and accumulates.
NIT1 deficiency is followed by electron-dense deposits in the walls of small and medium-sized cerebral arteries. The intermediate steps, including whether dGSH itself is deposited, are unknown.
dGSH accumulation is proposed to interfere with glutathione metabolism and cause redox damage. This is a hypothesis; patient fibroblasts show only an adaptive increase in mitochondrial SOD activity.

The small vessel disease presents with numerous, massively dilated perivascular spaces in the basal ganglia. A direct mechanistic link from the wall deposits to perivascular space dilation has not been shown.
edges.target: Massively Dilated Basal Ganglia Perivascular Spaces

edges.description: Non-lobar intracerebral hemorrhage in mid-adulthood is attributed to the small vessel disease; the vessel-wall lesion is the presumed substrate.
Movement disorders are the presenting feature and are attributed to the basal ganglia small vessel disease; the specific movement phenomenology is not given in the abstract.

The basal ganglia cavities of the French family are read by its authors as lacunar lesions, the same small-vessel lesion class as the dilated perivascular spaces of the later series. A direct link from the wall deposits to cavitation has not been shown.
Urinary dGSH excretion in the knockout matches the patient biochemical phenotype.
edges.limitations: The cited study reports only the metabolite; no cerebrovascular, perivascular-space or neurological phenotype of the knockout is reported there, so the model is not yet shown to reproduce the small vessel disease.

nodes.description: Deaminated glutathione (N-(4-oxoglutaryl)-L-cysteinylglycine) builds up in NIT1-deficient cells and is excreted in urine, where it is the diagnostic metabolite and the probable cause of a positive urine sulfite dipstick test. Transaminases, cytosolic and mitochondrial, are the main source of dGSH.
